messages.content:
## Bottom line

A cold-climate air-source heat pump can provide useful heat in a northern Minnesota winter, but “cold-climate” does not mean its capacity and efficiency stay constant as temperatures fall. The evidence I could verify supports treating it as a system to size for the house’s heat loss, with a deliberate plan for backup heat—not assuming any one advertised rating guarantees performance in prolonged extreme cold.

**Important research limitation:** I searched for the requested materials, but the fetch tool could not open several key PDFs: the NEEP specification and DOE Challenge documents were rejected as PDF content, and the PNNL report returned HTTP 403. I successfully opened and read three HTML sources in full: NEEP’s Version 4.0 announcement, a CEE Minnesota field-study page, and the IRS incentive page. That is **one fewer than the four full primary sources you requested**, and I can’t represent the PDF search snippets below as full-source verification.

## Cold-weather performance: what the available figures do—and don’t—say

- **NEEP:** A search result for NEEP’s older Version 2.0 specification reported a minimum **COP above 1.75 at 5°F**, at maximum capacity. It also said manufacturers report capacity and COP at 47°F, 17°F, and 5°F. This is a specification threshold, **not a typical performance result**. NEEP’s full Version 4.0 announcement was accessible, but it does not itself establish one capacity-retention or COP figure for all listed equipment.  
  Sources: [NEEP Version 4.0 announcement](https://neep.org/blog/neep-finalizes-version-40-cold-climate-air-source-heat-pump-specification); [older Version 2.0 specification PDF](https://neep.org/sites/default/files/resources/Cold%20Climate%20Air-source%20Heat%20Pump%20Specification-Version%202.0_0.pdf) (not readable through the fetch tool).

- **DOE Challenge:** Search results described a 5°F lab target of **100% of 47°F capacity**, with minimum COP targets of **2.1 or 2.4 depending on unit size**. Those are Challenge qualification targets, not a finding that all installed cold-climate systems achieve those figures. The DOE PDFs could not be opened directly here.  
  Sources: [DOE Challenge specification PDF](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2021-10/bto-cchp-tech-challenge-spec-102521.pdf); [DOE fact sheet PDF](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2021-11/bto-cchp-fact-sheet-102821.pdf).

- **Field performance:** A search result for a PNNL validation report described a **median COP of 1.9 in the 0–5°F temperature bin**. It also cautioned that the reported field COP excluded auxiliary-heat and defrost periods; only 8 of 22 sites had at least 10 hours of heating data below 0°F. I could not fetch that report, so treat these as **search-result figures, not independently checked report text**. They are not directly comparable to a lab rating or a whole-system seasonal result.  
  Source: [PNNL field-validation report PDF](https://www.pnnl.gov/main/publications/external/technical_reports/PNNL-37127.pdf) (fetch returned HTTP 403).

These figures do **not** establish a single “typical capacity retention at 5°F and below.” The NEEP table asks for model-specific capacity data, and the reported field COP is not a capacity-retention measurement. Ask contractors for the exact proposed outdoor unit’s capacity and COP at **5°F, 0°F, and the local design temperature**, and compare those with a room-by-room or otherwise documented heat-loss calculation for your house.

## Minnesota field experience and cost

CEE’s Minnesota field work is relevant, but it involved a small number of homes and different system configurations. Its project page describes six monitored homes, with a later update covering seven sites; the studies included propane-backup arrangements. The search result for the original study reported **26–40% lower annual energy costs** and **55–67% lower propane use** in certain ducted comparisons. Those are study-specific outcomes, not a guarantee for a 1,900-square-foot house or for today’s fuel and electricity prices.  
Source: [CEE field-assessment page](https://www.mncee.org/cold-climate-air-source-heat-pump-field-assessment-closed) (read in full); [original report PDF](https://www.mncee.org/sites/default/files/report-files/cold-climate_0.pdf) (PDF not accessible through the fetch tool).

A search result reported an average around **$14,000** for a small set of ducted installations, often including a new furnace. I could not verify that figure in the underlying report here, and it should **not** be treated as a current installed-cost estimate for your house. Installed cost depends substantially on equipment, ductwork, electrical work, backup integration, and whether the boiler remains. Get itemized bids that state what is included; don’t compare a heat-pump-only quote with one that includes backup or distribution-system work.

## Incentives right now

The IRS page I read says the federal **Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit (Section 25C) is unavailable for qualifying property placed in service after December 31, 2025**. A search result likewise reported that 2026 installations do not qualify under the current federal rule; the earlier 2025 credit was generally 30% of eligible cost, up to $2,000 for a qualifying heat pump. The prior-year amount is not an incentive for a 2026 installation.  
Source: [IRS: How to claim the residential energy-property credit](https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/how-to-claim-an-energy-efficient-home-improvement-tax-credit-residential-energy-property) (read in full); [IRS instructions](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i5695).

I did **not** verify current Minnesota, utility, or local incentives, so I can’t tell you which of those may be available for your home today.

## What remains uncertain for your house

The sources available in this run don’t settle the actual capacity coverage, operating cost, or backup requirement for your specific house. Those depend on the house’s heat loss, the proposed equipment’s low-temperature performance, the boiler’s role, and current propane and electricity prices. The main disagreement in the numbers above is not necessarily a contradiction: **NEEP and DOE figures are equipment qualification targets; the PNNL number is a limited field result using a different measurement basis.**

On **backup use during the coldest weather**, I can’t give a reliable amount—such as a percentage of heat or hours—from the accessible study material. That is guidance, not a report of how much backup those particular homes actually used on the coldest days. The earlier field figures about reduced propane use are seasonal study comparisons, not a coldest-day backup breakdown.

The PNNL result mentioned earlier is less useful for your specific question: its reported COP was a field-performance measure, not a measure of backup reliance, and the report could not be opened for verification. **Bottom line:** the CEE propane-backup homes are the most relevant comparison we have, but the available evidence does not quantify their backup use on the coldest days. For your boiler-based house, ask an installer to model the proposed heat pump against a documented house heat-loss calculation, show its capacity at local winter design temperature, and explain exactly when the existing boiler would take over.

messages.content:
I’d treat this as a **hybrid system**, not ask the heat pump to guarantee the house stays warm at −25°F.

- **Keep the propane boiler** and its existing hydronic distribution as the dependable cold-weather backup. Have the installer verify the boiler and distribution can meet the house’s heat loss at your local design temperature.
- **Add a cold-climate air-source heat pump** sized from a documented heat-loss calculation. If the house has suitable ducts, a ducted system may distribute heat broadly; without ducts, a strategically placed ductless system can provide heat to its zones, while the boiler continues serving the rest of the house. The best choice depends on the layout—not just the 1,900-square-foot area.
- Use **automatic controls** that favor the heat pump when it can meet the load, then bring on the boiler as the heat pump’s capacity falls or electricity becomes expensive. Have the contractor show the proposed unit’s capacity and operating limits at 5°F, 0°F, and −25°F; the earlier research did not establish typical capacity or COP at −25°F. I would not choose a switchover temperature without those equipment data and your propane/electricity prices.
- Treat **“grid strained” separately from “power outage.”** A hybrid system can reduce electric heating load by shifting heat to propane, but the boiler may still need electricity for its controls, ignition, and circulator pumps. If your requirement includes staying warm through an outage, ask about a properly sized generator or other backup power for those components, and confirm how the system will operate safely.

A roughly **$22,000 pre-incentive budget** is a useful bid constraint, but I can’t say this layout will fit it: the earlier research did not verify current installed costs or Minnesota/utility incentives. Request itemized bids that preserve the boiler and specify equipment, electrical work, controls, and any distribution changes. Compare each bid against the same heat-loss calculation and ask what the system does at −25°F—and during a power outage.

## Bottom line

A cold-climate air-source heat pump can provide useful heat in a northern Minnesota winter, but “cold-climate” does not mean its capacity and efficiency stay constant as temperatures fall. The evidence I could verify supports treating it as a system to size for the house’s heat loss, with a deliberate plan for backup heat—not assuming any one advertised rating guarantees performance in prolonged extreme cold.

**Important research limitation:** I searched for the requested materials, but the fetch tool could not open several key PDFs: the NEEP specification and DOE Challenge documents were rejected as PDF content, and the PNNL report returned HTTP 403. I successfully opened and read three HTML sources in full: NEEP’s Version 4.0 announcement, a CEE Minnesota field-study page, and the IRS incentive page. That is **one fewer than the four full primary sources you requested**, and I can’t represent the PDF search snippets below as full-source verification.

## Cold-weather performance: what the available figures do—and don’t—say

- **NEEP:** A search result for NEEP’s older Version 2.0 specification reported a minimum **COP above 1.75 at 5°F**, at maximum capacity. It also said manufacturers report capacity and COP at 47°F, 17°F, and 5°F. This is a specification threshold, **not a typical performance result**. NEEP’s full Version 4.0 announcement was accessible, but it does not itself establish one capacity-retention or COP figure for all listed equipment.  
  Sources: [NEEP Version 4.0 announcement](https://neep.org/blog/neep-finalizes-version-40-cold-climate-air-source-heat-pump-specification); [older Version 2.0 specification PDF](https://neep.org/sites/default/files/resources/Cold%20Climate%20Air-source%20Heat%20Pump%20Specification-Version%202.0_0.pdf) (not readable through the fetch tool).

- **DOE Challenge:** Search results described a 5°F lab target of **100% of 47°F capacity**, with minimum COP targets of **2.1 or 2.4 depending on unit size**. Those are Challenge qualification targets, not a finding that all installed cold-climate systems achieve those figures. The DOE PDFs could not be opened directly here.  
  Sources: [DOE Challenge specification PDF](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2021-10/bto-cchp-tech-challenge-spec-102521.pdf); [DOE fact sheet PDF](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2021-11/bto-cchp-fact-sheet-102821.pdf).

- **Field performance:** A search result for a PNNL validation report described a **median COP of 1.9 in the 0–5°F temperature bin**. It also cautioned that the reported field COP excluded auxiliary-heat and defrost periods; only 8 of 22 sites had at least 10 hours of heating data below 0°F. I could not fetch that report, so treat these as **search-result figures, not independently checked report text**. They are not directly comparable to a lab rating or a whole-system seasonal result.  
  Source: [PNNL field-validation report PDF](https://www.pnnl.gov/main/publications/external/technical_reports/PNNL-37127.pdf) (fetch returned HTTP 403).

These figures do **not** establish a single “typical capacity retention at 5°F and below.” The NEEP table asks for model-specific capacity data, and the reported field COP is not a capacity-retention measurement. Ask contractors for the exact proposed outdoor unit’s capacity and COP at **5°F, 0°F, and the local design temperature**, and compare those with a room-by-room or otherwise documented heat-loss calculation for your house.

## Minnesota field experience and cost

CEE’s Minnesota field work is relevant, but it involved a small number of homes and different system configurations. Its project page describes six monitored homes, with a later update covering seven sites; the studies included propane-backup arrangements. The search result for the original study reported **26–40% lower annual energy costs** and **55–67% lower propane use** in certain ducted comparisons. Those are study-specific outcomes, not a guarantee for a 1,900-square-foot house or for today’s fuel and electricity prices.  
Source: [CEE field-assessment page](https://www.mncee.org/cold-climate-air-source-heat-pump-field-assessment-closed) (read in full); [original report PDF](https://www.mncee.org/sites/default/files/report-files/cold-climate_0.pdf) (PDF not accessible through the fetch tool).

A search result reported an average around **$14,000** for a small set of ducted installations, often including a new furnace. I could not verify that figure in the underlying report here, and it should **not** be treated as a current installed-cost estimate for your house. Installed cost depends substantially on equipment, ductwork, electrical work, backup integration, and whether the boiler remains. Get itemized bids that state what is included; don’t compare a heat-pump-only quote with one that includes backup or distribution-system work.

## Incentives right now

The IRS page I read says the federal **Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit (Section 25C) is unavailable for qualifying property placed in service after December 31, 2025**. A search result likewise reported that 2026 installations do not qualify under the current federal rule; the earlier 2025 credit was generally 30% of eligible cost, up to $2,000 for a qualifying heat pump. The prior-year amount is not an incentive for a 2026 installation.  
Source: [IRS: How to claim the residential energy-property credit](https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/how-to-claim-an-energy-efficient-home-improvement-tax-credit-residential-energy-property) (read in full); [IRS instructions](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i5695).

I did **not** verify current Minnesota, utility, or local incentives, so I can’t tell you which of those may be available for your home today.

## What remains uncertain for your house

The sources available in this run don’t settle the actual capacity coverage, operating cost, or backup requirement for your specific house. Those depend on the house’s heat loss, the proposed equipment’s low-temperature performance, the boiler’s role, and current propane and electricity prices. The main disagreement in the numbers above is not necessarily a contradiction: **NEEP and DOE figures are equipment qualification targets; the PNNL number is a limited field result using a different measurement basis.**
Thanks. Which of those field results came from houses most like mine, and how much did they still lean on backup heat on the coldest days?

**The closest match is CEE’s Minnesota field study**, but it is only a partial match. It monitored six occupied Minnesota homes where natural gas was unavailable; **four used propane furnaces for backup**, and two used electric-resistance baseboards. That makes the propane-heated homes more relevant to your fuel situation than the broader field results—but they had **propane furnaces, not propane boilers**, and the source details available here don’t establish that any home was close to your 1,900 sq ft size. So I can’t call them close matches in house size or heating distribution. [CEE field-study page](https://www.mncee.org/cold-climate-air-source-heat-pump-field-assessment-closed)

On **backup use during the coldest weather**, I can’t give a reliable amount—such as a percentage of heat or hours—from the accessible study material. CEE’s page says a system may need backup to meet the load below **10°F** down to design conditions; it recommends prioritizing the heat pump so backup is used only when needed. That is guidance, not a report of how much backup those particular homes actually used on the coldest days. The earlier field figures about reduced propane use are seasonal study comparisons, not a coldest-day backup breakdown.

The PNNL result mentioned earlier is less useful for your specific question: its reported COP was a field-performance measure, not a measure of backup reliance, and the report could not be opened for verification. **Bottom line:** the CEE propane-backup homes are the most relevant comparison we have, but the available evidence does not quantify their backup use on the coldest days. For your boiler-based house, ask an installer to model the proposed heat pump against a documented house heat-loss calculation, show its capacity at local winter design temperature, and explain exactly when the existing boiler would take over.

Some context for the next step: our budget is roughly $22,000 before incentives, and one requirement from my partner is that the house stays heated at -25F even if the grid is strained. We also decided last week to keep the propane boiler as backup rather than remove it. With that in mind, what system layout would you suggest?

I’d treat this as a **hybrid system**, not ask the heat pump to guarantee the house stays warm at −25°F.

- **Keep the propane boiler** and its existing hydronic distribution as the dependable cold-weather backup. Have the installer verify the boiler and distribution can meet the house’s heat loss at your local design temperature.
- **Add a cold-climate air-source heat pump** sized from a documented heat-loss calculation. If the house has suitable ducts, a ducted system may distribute heat broadly; without ducts, a strategically placed ductless system can provide heat to its zones, while the boiler continues serving the rest of the house. The best choice depends on the layout—not just the 1,900-square-foot area.
- Use **automatic controls** that favor the heat pump when it can meet the load, then bring on the boiler as the heat pump’s capacity falls or electricity becomes expensive. Have the contractor show the proposed unit’s capacity and operating limits at 5°F, 0°F, and −25°F; the earlier research did not establish typical capacity or COP at −25°F. I would not choose a switchover temperature without those equipment data and your propane/electricity prices.
- Treat **“grid strained” separately from “power outage.”** A hybrid system can reduce electric heating load by shifting heat to propane, but the boiler may still need electricity for its controls, ignition, and circulator pumps. If your requirement includes staying warm through an outage, ask about a properly sized generator or other backup power for those components, and confirm how the system will operate safely.

A roughly **$22,000 pre-incentive budget** is a useful bid constraint, but I can’t say this layout will fit it: the earlier research did not verify current installed costs or Minnesota/utility incentives. Request itemized bids that preserve the boiler and specify equipment, electrical work, controls, and any distribution changes. Compare each bid against the same heat-loss calculation and ask what the system does at −25°F—and during a power outage.
